blocks.x: A no-theater description of Fleet Management System — Architecture & Trust: what ships first, what it touches at operational stores, how it is verified, and the per workflow metric we commit to moving against baseline.

The platform separates three planes. The data plane carries workload (medallion architecture with data contracts, tag-based access control with lineage, Kafka/Flink with exactly-once semantics); the control plane carries policy and orchestration (feature store, vector search, retrieval services, workload isolation and showback); the evidence plane carries audit, replay and conformity documentation — the plane most vendors skip and every regulator asks about.

blocks.x: Forge inherits platform controls from the customer landing zone and adds its own: contract enforcement, lineage capture, quality gates and privacy-tag-driven access. Every dataset carries its owner, SLA and classification — governance is system behavior, not committee minutes.

items: Sharing without exposure for data products
The control estate mapped to SOC 2 and ISO 27001 criteria, evidence produced continuously.
Sector rules translated into controls per jurisdiction — the mapping is data, reviewed when the regime moves.
AI-specific obligations mapped to controls — model risk, transparency and human oversight, owned by name.

blocks.x: The control plane is sized for enterprise scale: decision and orchestration paths carry published latency budgets, and the evidence plane writes append-only logs that never sit on the hot path.
The program dashboard tracks these by default, wired to your channels:

items: Spend per query attributed to the team that wrote it — the meter everyone can see.
Query latency measured at p95 from real workloads — the number users feel is the number reported.
Breakage restored and measured — the repair clock starts at alert, not at someone noticing.
Deployed inside your tenancy, your keys, your logs — the default for regulated estates.
Operated by us under contract — SLOs published, changes gated, your auditors given a walkthrough path.
Split by design: what must stay local stays local, what benefits from scale scales.

blocks.x: Connectivity is read-first by default and writes pass policy checks; every adapter documents its retries, its idempotency window and its audit trail.

items: Workloads land on the cheapest compute that still meets the latency budget.
Open table formats underneath everything we build, so your data never belongs to a vendor.
Tested, documented models with lineage exposure — the transform layer your analysts can actually read.
Events land in seconds, not overnight batches — the precondition for decisions that happen in the moment.
